title: Student’s t when s replaces σ
dek: t_ν is a Normal numerator over an independent χ²-based scale. You use it because s is random, not because the science is “small-n philosophy.” Degrees of freedom name that scale’s χ².
story: When σ is known and Yᵢ are iid Normal, Z = (Ȳ − μ) / (σ/√n) is exactly N(0,1). In a lab you almost never know σ. Replacing σ by the sample SD s gives T = (Ȳ − μ) / (s/√n). That extra randomness in s fattens the tails relative to Z. Under the Normal iid model, T ~ t_{n−1}. The move is studentisation, not a different philosophy of H₀.

Student’s t_ν can be built as Z / √(V/ν) with Z ~ N(0,1) independent of V ~ χ²_ν. The χ² in the denominator is why (n−1)s²/σ² ~ χ²_{n−1} for Normal data, and why the one-sample df is n−1 rather than n: s² is computed from residuals around Ȳ, one linear constraint. As ν → ∞, s concentrates (a variance LLN) and t_ν → N(0,1).

Six technical replicates of a log MIC do not become a z-interval because you are tired of tables. t_5 97.5% is about 2.57, not 1.96. Using z pretends s was σ. The SD-versus-SE plate already split s from s/√n; this plate is what happens to the Normal reference when the denominator is estimated.
deepTitle: df, heavier tails, and what is not a t
deep: One-sample: df = n − 1. Paired differences: df = number of pairs minus 1. Two-sample equal-variance: n₁ + n₂ − 2. Welch (unequal variance) uses a data-dependent df approximation — a different reference, still a t-shaped tail, not a licence to quote z.
Var(t_ν) = ν/(ν − 2) for ν > 2, larger than 1. That is the heavier-tail fact in one line. Critical values recede toward 1.96 as ν grows; they do not start there.

Robustness: the exact t law used iid Normal Y. A CLT can still justify a z or t approximation for Ȳ in large n without Normal Y, but then you are in approximation land (and sandwich/bootstrap SEs if dependence or heavy tails bite). Small n plus heavy tails is the regime where neither z nor t is a blessing.

A t test is a test that uses this reference. The distribution is not the test. Software printing “t = 2.1, df = 8, p = …” assumed a model for the scale. Caption the sampling unit (isolate, well, patient), not the column title.
z versus t is estimated scale versus known scale. It is not “Bayesian versus frequentist,” and it is not χ² (that is a sum of Normal squares, own plate).

formulas.label: Student’s t as a ratio
formulas.expression: T = Z / √(V/ν),   Z ~ N(0,1)  ⊥  V ~ χ²_ν   ⇒   T ~ t_ν
formulas.note: Independence of numerator and denominator is part of the definition.

formulas.label: One-sample studentised mean
formulas.note: Normal iid Y. s estimates σ; n−1 is the χ² df in s².

visual.caption: Same centre, three tails: N(0,1), t with tiny df (mass in the wings), and t with large df hugging the Normal. The extra spread is the price of estimating σ. It is not a different null hypothesis.

example.title: n = 6 log-MIC replicates, z versus t
example.setup: iid Normal model on log MIC. Ȳ = 0.40, s = 0.30, n = 6. H₀: μ = 0.20 (a process target). Two people studentise; one uses z = 1.96 as if s were σ.

steps.title: SE and T
steps.body: se = s/√n = 0.30/√6 ≈ 0.122. T = (0.40 − 0.20)/0.122 ≈ 1.63. The statistic is the same whether you later compare it to z or to t_5. The reference changes.

steps.title: df
steps.body: One-sample df = 6 − 1 = 5, because (n−1)s²/σ² ~ χ²_5 in this model. A two-sided 95% t_5 critical value is about 2.57, not 1.96. |1.63| does not reject at 5% on t_5; pretending s = σ makes the tail look rarer than it is.

steps.title: What n = 6 did not buy
steps.body: A CLT story for Ȳ might be a stretch at n = 6 if log MIC is skewed. Switching from z to t repairs estimated scale, not a heavy-tailed parent. If the well-to-well errors are not even iid, neither reference is the adult object.

example.takeaway: s in the denominator changes the reference to t. df counts how that s was built.

check.prompt: In the Normal iid model, we use a t reference for (Ȳ − μ)/(s/√n) rather than N(0,1) because:
choices: The null hypothesis is a different scientific question when n is small
s is a random estimate of σ, so the studentised ratio has heavier tails than Z
Variance is infinite by definition whenever s is used
t is the Bayesian posterior for μ with no prior
check.answer: s is a random estimate of σ, so the studentised ratio has heavier tails than Z
check.why: Studentisation is extra randomness in the scale. H₀ did not change species.

whyWrong.The null hypothesis is a different scien: H₀ is still a statement about μ. The sampling law of the statistic changed.
whyWrong.Variance is infinite by definition whene: s² estimates a finite σ²; t_ν has finite variance once ν > 2.
whyWrong.t is the Bayesian posterior for μ with n: t here is a frequentist sampling law. A posterior needs a prior (own Bayes plates).

check.prompt: One-sample t, n = 16, Ȳ = 12, s = 8, H₀: μ = 10. The t statistic is:
check.why: se = 8/√16 = 2. T = (12 − 10)/2 = 1. df would be 15 if you needed a tail; the statistic itself is 1.

whyWrong.2: That is the SE, or (12−10) without dividing by se.
whyWrong.0.25: That divided by s instead of se, or used n not √n.

check.prompt: On the density plate, the t_3 curve is the widest because:
choices: Small df means the χ² scale in the denominator is noisy, so more probability sits in the tails
t_3 has a larger mean than N(0,1)
Large df always has the heaviest tails
The plate is a χ² on CFU
check.answer: Small df means the χ² scale in the denominator is noisy, so more probability sits in the tails
check.why: t_3 is Z over a noisy √(V/3). t_30 has already almost recovered the Normal.

whyWrong.t_3 has a larger mean than N(0,1): All three curves are centred at 0 in the plate.
whyWrong.Large df always has the heaviest tails: Opposite: t_ν → z as ν grows.
whyWrong.The plate is a χ² on CFU: χ² is a different named law (sum of squares).
